title: friction-garden-hacklog-nov-2029
content:
Context: quick-hack log for a handful of persistent low-signal but high-friction customer threads surfaced in field calls (Nov week 1). This doc collects raw quotes, small-target probes, and a prioritized microfix backlog intended for a fast eng + CS spike (1-2 sprints). Not a polished roadmap—meant to be actionable and small-batch deployable.

Topline synthesis (one-paragraph): customers repeatedly run into unpredictable latency spikes on bursty short-chat workloads and see higher token costs when prompts include many short repeated system messages. They ask for: 1) a transparent, low-friction knob to prefer lower-latency model variants when available; 2) more aggressive suggestions for kv/prefix caching per-route with sample cost impact; and 3) a small syntactic normalization that trims duplicate assistant/system headers to reduce token count. Most prefer surface-level fixes that are safe and reversible (canary) over big infra changes.

Representative customer snippets (redacted):
- "We see the service pop from 80ms to 700ms for 1 in 20 calls and it kills our UX—no pattern in logs right now." — mid-market SaaS PM
- "Every time we stitch templates the token bill spikes; we have 30 repeated system lines that could be cached if only we had a router-side option." — AI platform engineer
- "Can you just give us a fallback param so we hit a cheaper variant when load is high? We can handle tiny quality drops." — startup CTO

Observed patterns and quick hypotheses:
- Pattern A: Short requests (under 80 tokens) with high concurrency see tail latency because they fall through batching thresholds and incur kernel startup variance. Hypothesis: Make a continuous-batching hill-climb parameter tunable per-customer to reduce tail latency for short requests.
- Pattern B: Templates with repeated system content cause high per-response token count and prevent prefix caching because the runtime treats each request as unique. Hypothesis: a lightweight normalization/ID scheme (hash repeated headers + replace) could enable prefix-KV cache hits across requests.
- Pattern C: Customers want controlled graceful degradation: prefer a policy to route to a cheaper model variant on overload. Hypothesis: expose a route-level policy 'prefer-lower-cost-fallback' that triggers when estimated queue delay > threshold.

Microprobes (ranked by expected impact / engineering cost):
1) Token-trim shim (low cost): introduce server-side normalization that collapses consecutive identical system/assistant lines and trims trailing whitespace in prompt templates. Risks: minimal; testing: regression suite for chat formatting. Owner: CS+DX spike -> eng spike. Estimated effort: 1 engineer, 3 days. Expected impact: 3-7% token reduction for templated workflows.
2) Route-level fallback flag (medium cost): add boolean policy prefer_lower_variant with a soft-threshold (ms delay) decision at router. Requires light routing metric and a safe canary rollout. Owner: platform + routing team. Estimated effort: 2 engineers, 2 sprints. Expected impact: reduces outage surface and cost during capacity events; UX improvement for bursty customers.
3) Continuous-batching tunables (higher cost): expose a per-customer knob to bias batching behavior for short sequences (e.g., min-batch-delay-ms). Requires careful load-testing and kernel profiling. Owner: serving-runtime. Estimated effort: 3-4 engineers, 3 sprints. Expected impact: lower tail latency for small requests, potential throughput tradeoffs.
4) Prefix-KV normalization experiment (research spike): a route-moderated normalization that canonicalizes repeated header blocks and assigns a shared KV cache key. Requires changes to KV cache keying and replay safety checks. Owner: applied-ml + runtime. Estimated effort: 1-2 engineers, research + 2 sprints to prototype. Expected impact: large cost savings for templated customers but complexity high.

Quick fixes we can ship in <2 weeks: 
- Implement Token-trim shim (probe 1).
- Add a documented recommendation + sample code in Console for customers to pre-hash and reuse system messages (workaround).
- Short-term alert: add monitoring dashboard card for route-level 95/99 latencies for requests <100 tokens.

Risk notes and open questions:
- Prefix-KV normalization might interact poorly with function-calling or tool-invocations where header semantics matter; need safety tests.
- Route-level fallback could cause quality regressions that erode trust. Must pair with explicit per-route opt-in and measurable rollback.
- Batching tunable needs to consider Dedicated vs Hosted differences; Dedicated customers may want different defaults.

Proposed acceptance criteria for probes:
- Token-trim shim live canary on 5% of customer traffic with automated token-billing delta measured; must show >=2% median token reduction for templated routes without increased errors.
- prefer_lower_variant flag implemented behind feature gate; in canary mode, fallbacks should not exceed 10% of requests for an opt-in route and have a rollback path.
- Batching knob must demonstrate median 95th latency improvement for <100-token requests in staging load test without >5% throughput loss.

Owner / next steps:
- (Today) CS: surface top 6 customers that reported spikes and invite to a 30-min spike review (Maya).
- (48h) Eng spike: implement token-trim shim prototype in sandbox (Adrian).
- (1 week) Monitoring: add short-request latency cards and billing delta chart (SRE / Observability team).
- (2 wks) Run canary and collect billing / latency deltas; reconvene and decide on route-level fallback spike.

Short backlog (JIRA keys):
- JIRA-INF-3287: token-trim shim implementation (spike)
- JIRA-INF-3291: per-route prefer_lower_variant feature gate
- JIRA-INF-3302: batching-tunable config + load test
- JIRA-INF-3315: prefix-kv normalization research spike

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Could prototype fallback by allowing customers to supply a ranked model list in SDK; router performs cheaper-model preference client-side until we have a server-side policy.
- Consider an SDK helper to compress repeated system metadata into a single compact token (not strictly canonicalization but pragmatic).

Appendix: Quick customer mapping (for outreach)
- Customer A (mid-market CRM): high short-tail latency; willing to test prefer_lower_variant. Contact: Leah R.
- Customer B (document automation startup): heavy templating, prime candidate for token-trim + prefix-KV research. Contact: Marco T.
- Customer C (enterprise legal search): sensitive to quality—will only accept opt-in canary for fallback. Contact: Priya S.

This is intentionally a lightweight, iterative hacklog. If we get buy-in on the token-trim probe and monitoring, we can move the bigger probes into the next quarterly engineering plan.
